newsitem.title: USA: Climate change deal would hurt economies, study says.
newsitem.headline: Climate change deal would hurt economies, study says.

text.p: An international deal to reduce heat-trapping air pollution could trim 2 to 5 percent off the economic growth of industrialised countries in coming decades, economists said on Thursday in a report released by an industry coalition.
Among the hardest-hit would be Canada, while among the least affected would be Germany and Britain, the study by Charles River Associates said.

The United States would lose 2.44 percent off projected growth in gross domestic output by 2030 under a plan to reduce industrial emissions to 1990 levels by 2010 and stabilise them at that level through 2030, the report said.
It would lose 3.31 percent off projected GDP growth under a plan to reduce emissions to 90 percent of 1990 levels by 2010 and maintain that through 2030, it said.
The Global Climate Coalition, made up largely of oil and coal industries, released the analysis of emissions reductions on 80 countries.
The GCC opposes measures to sharply reduce fossil fuel emissions, called greenhouse gases, which scientists say are contributing to global warming.
The Charles River study said economies of many developing nations also would be hurt under the two pollution reduction scenarios, as economic slowdowns in industrialised countries would reduce trade.
"The entire world ... is connected through international trade, and all countries will be affected if economic growth slows in industrial countries," the report said.

This report came several weeks after some 2,300 economists, including eight Nobel Prize-winners, signed a statement saying measures could be taken to stem global warming which would not lower U.S. living standards and could improve the economy over the longer term.
The Clinton administration is to release its economic analysis soon, possibly next month.
Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth this week said industry reports for the most part have overstated costs and made unrealistic assumptions.
But Bill O'Keefe, GCC chairman, at a new conference said it "is an illusion and a fallacy" to think steep emissions cuts could be made without economic harm.
O'Keefe also said the report "shows the danger of conducting negotiations without a good factual basis."
The United States in global climate negotiations has called for binding emissions targets for industrialised countries, but has not yet recommended specific numerical targets or timetables.
